items.title: 8.15 Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium

source_refs.note: Topic 8.15, printed page 182 (Figure 8.3, carried by the Le Chatelier original).

blocks.title: Catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself being consumed. It does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium constant of a reaction; it speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is attained, so the yield of the reaction stays the same.

A catalyst provides a new path of lower activation energy. On a graph of potential energy against reaction coordinate the maximum of the curve is lower in the presence of a catalyst: the activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction, Ea, is replaced by a smaller Ea' for the catalysed one, while the energies of reactants and products, and so delta H, are unchanged.

blocks.alt: Energy (y) against reaction coordinate (x). Two humped curves start at the reactant level and end at the lower product level. The taller curve (uncatalyzed) and the lower curve (catalyzed) each peak at an activated state. A double arrow Ea (uncatalyzed reaction) runs from the reactant level to the upper peak, a double arrow E'a (catalyzed reaction) from the reactant level to the lower peak, and ΔH between the reactant and product levels.
